newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu faces Likud critics on Arafat meeting.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu faces Likud critics on Arafat meeting.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu weathered criticism at a Likud party congress on Thursday over his landmark meeting with PLO head Yasser Arafat.
But he vowed to take a hard line in peace talks with the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO), which his party had refused to recognise until his meeting with Arafat on Wednesday.

After Netanyahu threatened to fire ministers who did not toe his line on peace moves, Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon and Science Minister Binyamin Begin, the most hawkish members of his cabinet, made clear they had no fear of being sacked.

Netanyahu began his speech with a party-pleasing broadside at former prime minister Shimon Peres, who he defeated in May elections, in which he rejected the PLO's goal of a state and hailed Jewish settlement of the West Bank and Gaza Strip.

"You can dream every night...And you will still wake up every morning and see: There is no Palestinian state, there is no Palestinian state, there is not and there will not be a Palestinian state," he said to applause.
"And Jewish settlement in Judea and Samaria (the West Bank) will live, will thrive, will exist forever," he added. Palestinians say settlement must stop.
In answer to a heckler from the audience, Netanyahu said: "Yes, yes. Also in the Gaza Strip, in Gush Katif, certainly."

Gush Katif is the name of a block of Jewish settlements in the Gaza Strip, the rest of which has been handed over to Palestinian rule under interim peace deals cut by the previous government. Netanyahu added he had expressed his commitment to settlement in the meeting with Arafat.
"Whoever comes with complaints now didn't have to join the coalition and didn't have to join the government...There is only one prime minister," Netanyahu said.
Earlier in an interview with Israel television, asked if he would fire ministers who did not fall into line with his policy, Netanyahu had said: "If necessary, yes."
Sharon, long a champion of Jewish settlement and who said on Wednesday the Arafat meeting was a mistake, was not cowed by the threat, making a veiled one of his own.
"It is possible to replace a minister...governments can also be replaced," Sharon, who has in the past referred to Arafat as a war criminal, said in his speech.
The party convention, scheduled before the Arafat meeting to deal with internal matters, was overshadowed by the handshake on Wednesday between the right-wing Israeli leader and PLO chief.

"I did everything so this man could betray me and my friends...What right did he have to go and shake the hand of this killer of children," one member of the hundreds-strong central committee screamed on Israel Radio.
But sentiments in the hall were mixed.
Backers of the meeting, like Likud member of parliament Meir Sheetreet, said Netanyahu was pragmatic and would ensure that a deal satisfying right-wing principles would result from negotiations.
